title: Make it fast, and prove it
goal: Almost every portfolio repository has an architecture. Almost none has a measurement. A before and after table on the authorisation path is the one line on your CV another candidate cannot copy without doing the work.
startWith: Step 14 finished. You optimise against timers you already trust, or you optimise against noise.

newIdeas.plain: A closed load model keeps N users in flight and waits for each response, so a slow system simply receives less load and hides its own problem. An open model arrives at a fixed rate whatever the system is doing, which is how real payment traffic behaves. Use the open model, or your numbers flatter you.

The measurement bug where a stalled request stops the load generator sending, so the stall never appears in the percentiles. It is why a tool reporting a clean p99 can be sitting on a two second pause. Gatling with an open injection profile avoids it.

Java 21 onward gives you threads the JVM schedules itself, so a request blocked on the database no longer occupies an operating system thread. For a service that spends its life waiting on IO, which is every payment service, it can change the throughput ceiling without changing the code.
A stacked view of where the CPU actually spent its time, sampled from the running JVM. Wide bar means expensive. It replaces the guess about which method is slow with a picture of which one is.

proof.expect: Two runs, same profile, and a p99 that moved for a reason you can name.
proof.note: Record the baseline before you change anything. A number you cannot compare to is not a result.

doneWhen: The README carries a table of p50, p95, p99 and throughput before and after, each row traced to the specific change that moved it.

tasks.do: Write the load profile before you touch any code
tasks.why: The optimisation you feel like doing and the optimisation the system needs are rarely the same one. The baseline is what tells them apart, and you can only capture it once.
tasks.how: Model the authorisation path as an open injection profile: a fixed arrival rate, held long enough that the JIT has warmed and the connection pool has settled. Discard the first thirty seconds. Record p50, p95, p99 and achieved throughput, and commit the result file so the comparison survives your memory.

blocks.label: scripts/load-auth.sh
blocks.body:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
LABEL="${1:-baseline}"

./mvnw -q -pl load gatling:test \
  -Dgatling.simulationClass=io.ledgerflow.load.AuthorizeSimulation \
  -DrateRps="${RATE:-200}" -DdurationSec="${DURATION:-180}"

mkdir -p docs/perf
cp -r load/target/gatling/authorizesimulation-* "docs/perf/${LABEL}"
echo "recorded docs/perf/${LABEL}"

blocks.label: load: AuthorizeSimulation.java

check.expect: A committed baseline you can point a later run at.

tasks.do: Find the bottleneck instead of guessing at it
tasks.why: Everyone guesses the database. It is often the outbox poll, the JSON serialiser or a pool sized for a laptop. Two hours with a profiler will save you a week of optimising the wrong method.
tasks.how: Attach async-profiler to the running service while the load is on and take a CPU flame graph and a wall-clock one. Read the wall-clock graph first: a payment service spends its life waiting, so the CPU picture alone will mislead you. Then ask Postgres what it actually ran, using pg_stat_statements ordered by total time rather than by call count.

blocks.label: Flame graph off the running JVM
blocks.body:
PID=$(jps -l | grep ledger-service | cut -d' ' -f1)

# wall clock first: this service waits more than it computes
asprof -d 60 -e wall -f docs/perf/wall.html "$PID"
asprof -d 60 -e cpu  -f docs/perf/cpu.html  "$PID"

blocks.label: Ask the database what it really ran
blocks.body:
docker exec -it lf-postgres psql -U ledgerflow -d ledger -c "
  SELECT calls,
         round(total_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS total_ms,
         round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)  AS mean_ms,
         left(query, 90) AS query
  FROM pg_stat_statements
  ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
  LIMIT 10;"

check.expect: You can name the top two costs, and neither of them is a guess.

tasks.do: Fix the top two, one at a time, measuring between them
tasks.why: Changing three things and rerunning once tells you the total moved and nothing about which change moved it. That is the difference between an anecdote and a result you can defend in an interview.
tasks.how: Take the largest cost first. The usual winners on this path are an outbox poll fetching one row per round trip when it could claim a batch, a missing partial index on the unpublished rows, a connection pool sized without reference to the database max, and an N+1 across postings. Change one, rerun the same profile, record it, then move to the next.

blocks.label: ledger: claim a batch instead of a row at a time
blocks.body:
@Query(value = """
    SELECT * FROM outbox
    WHERE published_at IS NULL
    ORDER BY id
    LIMIT :batch
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    """, nativeQuery = true)
List<OutboxRow> claimBatch(@Param("batch") int batch);

blocks.label: The index that keeps that poll flat as the table grows
blocks.body:
-- Partial: the outbox is almost entirely published rows, and indexing
-- those costs write time to buy nothing.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_outbox_unpublished
    ON outbox (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

blocks.label: Rerun the identical profile and record it

check.expect: One directory per change, so every row of the final table has a run behind it.

tasks.do: Run the same load on virtual threads and on platform threads
tasks.why: It is one line of configuration and it produces a number about a language feature every interviewer is currently curious about. It is also a genuine test of whether you understand what your service spends its time doing.
tasks.how: Turn on virtual threads, rerun the identical profile, and record it beside the platform thread run. Then look for the case that spoils it: a synchronized block held across a blocking call pins the carrier thread and gives back the ceiling you just bought. Finding one in your own code and writing down what you did about it is worth more than the speedup.

blocks.label: Look for pinning before you believe the number
blocks.body:
# every pinning event, with the stack that caused it
java -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full -jar ledger-service/target/ledger-service.jar

check.expect: Either no pinning, or a named cause and a note on what you changed.

tasks.do: Put the table in the README, above the architecture diagram
tasks.why: A reader gives the repository about forty seconds. Architecture is what they expected. A measured improvement with the reason next to it is what makes them read the rest, and it is the sentence that ends up on the CV.
tasks.how: One table. Columns for p50, p95, p99 and throughput. One row per change, each naming what moved and why. Say what the load was and on what hardware, because a number without its conditions reads as a number somebody made up.

blocks.label: README.md
blocks.body:
## Authorisation path, measured

Open model, 200 requests per second sustained for 180s, single node,
Postgres 17 in Docker, 8 core laptop. Full runs in `docs/perf/`.

| Change                          |  p50 |  p95 |   p99 | tps |
|---------------------------------|-----:|-----:|------:|----:|
| Baseline                        |      |      |       |     |
| Outbox claims a batch of 100    |      |      |       |     |
| Partial index on unpublished    |      |      |       |     |
| Virtual threads                 |      |      |       |     |

Each row is a single change, measured against the row above it.

check.expect: The numbers are the first thing on the page after the one line description.

lessons.title: Profile, don't guess
lessons.teach: Run the service with Run with Profiler and load it. A flame graph settles where the time goes in one run; a guess costs you a day of optimising the wrong method.
lessons.fallbackTip: Ultimate only. Community: async-profiler attached by pid.
